{"id": "50:27/q08", "question": "What does the speaker deny in ما أطغيته?", "turns_on": "Whether the denial concerns Satan's coercion or influence, or an angel's allegedly unfair record and timing.", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q08/p1", "position": "Satan denies forcing or independently causing the person's error; he only invited, whispered, embellished, or encouraged what the person chose.", "reasons": "Muqatil says Satan lacked power to mislead without God's authority; Wahidi reports his claim that the man was already forsaken by God. Al-Qurazi specifically denies compulsion. Qushayri, Tabarsi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalılı, and Tabatabai emphasize the man's choice. Tabarsi, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, Alusi, Wahidi Wajiz, Kuranyolu, Study Quran, and Tabatabai compare 14:22: Satan had no authority beyond a call that people answered and should blame themselves. Kuranyolu includes that neither side can rescue the other and Satan denied their association of him with God. Bursevi cites a hadith contrasting the messenger's inability to guide everyone with Iblis's mere adornment. Ibn Ashur says the denial answers the suspicion created by close association. Islahi says the denial does not deny Satan's call toward error: in 14:22 Satan admits both making false promises and calling people, while they responded by choice."}, {"id": "50:27/q08/p2", "position": "The companion denies leading the person astray or making him disbelieve.", "reasons": "Tabari and Nahhas specify transgression into disbelief. Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, and Elmalılı word it as denial of misguidance or seduction. Ibn Atiyya says a general denial of causal influence is false, since Satan whispered and beautified evil."}, {"id": "50:27/q08/p3", "position": "The recording angel denies adding to or prematurely making the record, or hastening the person.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the angel recorded only words and deeds actually committed; Qushayri says only after the slip. Al-Farra's favored angel account denies both hastening and adding. The charges vary: adding entries, barring repentance, or rushing the man into error."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q09", "question": "Who is the person referred to by the object pronoun in أطغيته?", "turns_on": "Whether the exchange is between external companions and a human, or between appetites and conscious reason.", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q09/p1", "position": "The accused human, identified by some as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi.", "reasons": "Muqatil names al-Walid and says he lived in prolonged loss. Thalabi and Qurtubi report Ibn Abbas and Muqatil naming al-Walid in the angel version; the other accounts speak of the condemned disbeliever or human companion."}, {"id": "50:27/q09/p2", "position": "The person's faculty of conscious, controlling reason.", "reasons": "Asad reads the object pronoun as him or it, referring to reason in his account of appetites speaking."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q10", "question": "Why does the companion invoke the person's prior distant error?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q10/p1", "position": "The person was already deeply astray and freely receptive to evil, so the companion's prompting did not compel or originate his transgression.", "reasons": "Tabari and Nahhas describe a path away from guidance and truth. Wahidi reports Muqatil's detail that he was forsaken by God. Baghawi says he would not return; Baydawi and Bursevi say temptation works on unstable judgment inclined to wickedness. Ibn Kathir says he welcomed falsehood and resisted truth. Biqai says his pervasive disposition made him rush toward what angers God without the slightest prompting. Ibn Ashur reads كان as original and enduring, compares the disavowal in 2:166, and argues a mere follower is not so firmly established as an independent investigator. Tabatabai and Study Quran assign responsibility to the human who accepted suggestion. Asad instead applies the point to the conscious mind's departure from moral truth, explaining 50:24–25. Bursevi quotes Attar's Persian couplet of unsatisfied hunger and the unrewarded sieve as an illustration. Islahi says the man had ceased seeking guidance because he was so far from truth, leaving him vulnerable to Satan under God's established practice."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q11", "question": "What does كان convey about the person's misguidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q11/p1", "position": "The misguidance was original and enduring in the person's makeup.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the perfect verb establishes this duration; his reading of بعيد reinforces it."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q12", "question": "What does ضلال بعيد convey?", "turns_on": "Whether distance is from guidance and truth or, in the inward reading, from unity and innate light.", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q12/p1", "position": "Error far from the path of guidance or truth.", "reasons": "Tabari describes departure from guidance; Nahhas and Baghawi from truth; Ibn al-Jawzi and others gloss the phrase as far from guidance. Muqatil associates it with prolonged worldly loss. Ibn Ashur says distance is a metaphor like a distant place or time and echoes 4:116. Islahi explains the distance from truth as reaching the point where the man no longer sought guidance."}, {"id": "50:27/q12/p2", "position": "Distance from unity and original nature, with the soul turned to the lower realm and veiled in darkness.", "reasons": "Qashani's inward account says this condition makes satanic whispering preferable to angelic inspiration; he compares 14:22."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q13", "question": "What does بعيد add to the description of misguidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q13/p1", "position": "It intensifies the error as extreme, entrenched, and difficult to reverse.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says return to guidance was difficult. Ibn Ashur treats distance as metaphorical, compares 4:116, and says it reinforces the enduring force of كان. Islahi says the distance had become so great that the man no longer sought guidance and was vulnerable to Satan."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q14", "question": "What does the companion's denial teach about responsibility and causation?", "turns_on": "Whether denial of compulsion also excludes Satan's causal role through suggestion, and how that role relates to divine creation.", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q14/p1", "position": "Each person answers for accepting evil; Satan could invite, but could not force the choice.", "reasons": "Tabarsi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, and Tabatabai make the distinction between invitation and acceptance; 14:22 repeatedly supplies the parallel. Study Quran says people would not heed Satan unless already astray. Jishumi says God justly holds each accountable and wrongs no one by disputing on the basis of what He knows. Bursevi's cited hadith says even the messenger cannot guide everyone by his own power, and Iblis only adorns. Islahi says Satan is assigned to those heedless of God's remembrance under God's established practice; Satan's admitted false promises and call in 14:22 still left people free to respond, while prior distance from truth made the man vulnerable."}, {"id": "50:27/q14/p2", "position": "Satan did cause transgression by whispering and beautifying evil, while God created it under His prior decree.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says Satan's denial is false if made general; God's creation by decree is just and admits no other lord."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q15", "question": "What does the quarrel show about companions at judgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q15/p1", "position": "Companions disown one another and try to shift blame when judgment comes.", "reasons": "Tabari states the lesson and reports Ibn Zayd and Abu Imran explaining the companion's words as disavowal. Baghawi and Ibn Kathir say Satan disowns the unbeliever. Study Quran reports Tabari's innocence interpretation and compares Satan's disavowal and fear of God in 59:16. Ibn Ashur compares 2:166. Ibn Qutayba links pairing wrongdoers and companions to Arab practice of pairing camels and to 37:22 and 44:54; Wahidi compares the mutual blame in 37:27–33. Tabatabai recalls the gathering in 37:22. Islahi says each criminal blames Satan after entering Hell and compares the disavowal to 14:21, where the weak ask their powerful leaders for protection and those leaders say they would have guided them if God had guided them."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q16", "question": "What does the exchange signify in an inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q16/p1", "position": "It depicts conflict among inner faculties, especially estimative and intellectual powers, and opposing impulses such as anger and desire.", "reasons": "Qashani says the dialogue is an imaginative form that fixes its meaning in the heart. The powers cooperate when satisfied, but blame one another in loss because each seeks its own benefit and is veiled from unity. Distance from innate light and attraction to the lower realm make satanic whispering effective instead of angelic inspiration; he cites 14:22 and regards the sinner's acquired kinship with the devil as his fault."}]}
{"id": "50:27/q17", "question": "What reports are cited to illuminate companions and the quarrel?", "turns_on": "The reports address different aspects: the companion's identity and mutual attack at judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q17/p1", "position": "Everyone has a jinn companion; God helped the Prophet against his, and it submitted and urged only good.", "reasons": "Abd al-Razzaq and al-Durr transmit the report from the Prophet."}, {"id": "50:27/q17/p2", "position": "Haritha saw the people of Hell attacking one another, and the Prophet approved his observation.", "reasons": "Qashani transmits Haritha's report and says the Prophet also approved the devil's assertion that the man was already far astray."}]}

Islahi says the passage moves from the criminals' casting into Hell and mutual cursing to the blessings prepared for the righteous."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q01", "question": "How is يومَ connected grammatically to the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "The proposed governor or appositional antecedent: the day in 52:9 or 52:11, an implied saying, speech in 52:14, دافع, or لواقع; Makkī disputes the last verb's governance.", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q01/p1", "position": "It is an apposition to the preceding يومئذ, the day of woe for the deniers in 52:11.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī identify يومئذ as the antecedent; Rāzī relates it to the day promised in 52:11. Samīn allows this alongside another antecedent. Elmalılı says only that it replaces the preceding day expression."}, {"id": "52:13/q01/p2", "position": "It is an apposition to يوم تمور, the day the sky heaves in 52:9.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī, Samīn and Bursevī give the day when the sky heaves as antecedent; Ālūsī cites 52:9, and Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the apposition inclusive. Elmalılı leaves his preceding day unspecified."}, {"id": "52:13/q01/p3", "position": "It is a time adverb for an understood saying that introduces the next verse's speech.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Samīn posit an implied saying before هذه النار; Bursevī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı likewise attach the time to the quoted speech, with Elmalılı saying it explains the woe."}, {"id": "52:13/q01/p4", "position": "It is governed by the following statement in 52:14: on that day they are told this is the fire they denied.", "reasons": "Rāzī regards this as the plainest construction and contrasts it with apposition to the earlier day."}, {"id": "52:13/q01/p5", "position": "It is accusative under دافع in the preceding verse.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this parse from al-Ḥawfī."}, {"id": "52:13/q01/p6", "position": "It depends on لواقع, with ما له من دافع interrupting its governor and complement parenthetically.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this parse. He also reports Makkī's assertion that واقع cannot govern يوم, without an argument for that restriction."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q02", "question": "What does يُدَعُّونَ mean here?", "turns_on": "The forceful-pushing sense of the doubled verb, the light reading from calling, or Māwardī's proposed cursing by the wardens.", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q02/p1", "position": "The deniers are shoved or driven harshly and forcefully toward or into Hell, with coercion and humiliation.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Qatāda describe forced driving; Ibn ʿAbbās specifies their necks, while Mujāhid also says from behind. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk stresses coercion. Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Zayd, Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī compare 107:2, the pushing away of an orphan; Majāz cites Arab usage daʿa fī qafāhu and a light orphan verb, citing 2:107. Al-Layth cites a famine poem about pushing an orphan; Māwardī cites rajaz. Ibn al-Aʿrābī explains الدفر as pushing. Qatāda's version can emphasize violent rousing or hurrying. Samīn relates the common form to دفع and specifies pushing in the chest. Bursevī evokes shoving a stumbling person. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers harsh, rebuking coercion over mere deprivation of an orphan's right, since no right is being denied here. ʿIṣlāḥī adds hatred and worldly mockery; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes frightened people falling back and angels shoving them forward. Qāshānī adds dragging. The common form is doubled; Jishumī compares ṣakka yaṣukku ṣakkan."}, {"id": "52:13/q02/p2", "position": "They are called or summoned to the Fire.", "reasons": "Abū Rajāʾ and other named readers use a light form from دعاء; Qurtubī says the keepers then point out the denied Fire. Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn say they are told to come or enter; Bayḍāwī, Ālūsī, Rāzī and Study Quran report calling, with the noun explained as a circumstantial expression or great calling."}, {"id": "52:13/q02/p3", "position": "Hell's wardens call down curses on the condemned.", "reasons": "Māwardī offers this as a third possible sense after forceful pushing and driving."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q03", "question": "Does دعّ derive from a call to a stumbling person?", "turns_on": "Whether al-Rāghib's call to a stumbling person explains the verse's forceful pushing.", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q03/p1", "position": "Yes; its root began as the call دع دع to a stumbling person.", "reasons": "Samīn attributes this derivation to al-Rāghib but judges it remote from this verse's sense."}, {"id": "52:13/q03/p2", "position": "That derivation is remote from the sense here.", "reasons": "Samīn objects to al-Rāghib's proposed origin; his own explanation derives the common forceful form from دفع."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q04", "question": "How is يُدَعُّونَ دَعًّا read?", "turns_on": "Doubling versus lightening the verb's ʿayn changes its derivation from pushing to calling; reports also discuss the cognate noun's form and grammar.", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q04/p1", "position": "The common reading doubles the ʿayn, giving the forceful-pushing sense.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls it the majority reading and compares ṣakka yaṣukku ṣakkan. Samīn describes open dāl and doubled ʿayn. ʿIṣlāḥī treats the established reading in the present muṣḥaf as authoritative for interpreting verses and words, arguing that alternative readings lose eloquence, purpose and wisdom."}, {"id": "52:13/q04/p2", "position": "A light reading takes the verb from calling or summoning, and some accounts read دعاء as its accusative circumstantial expression.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya name Abū Rajāʾ; Ibn ʿAṭiyya specifies still dāl and open ʿayn. Qurtubī adds Ibn al-Sumayqa. Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn add ʿAlī, al-Sulamī and Zayd ibn ʿAlī. Ālūsī names Zayd, al-Sulamī and Abū Rajāʾ and calls the noun circumstantial. Rāzī explicitly reports دعاء as accusative circumstantial; Bayḍāwī and Study Quran explain the resulting summons, the latter as a great calling."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q05", "question": "What happens as the deniers are brought to Hell?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q05/p1", "position": "Hell's keepers bind the deniers and force them into the Fire, commonly face-first and prodded from behind.", "reasons": "Muqātil says this follows judgment: hands shackled to necks, forelocks tied to feet behind their backs, then a face-first push and the announcement of the Fire they denied. Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī and Ibn al-Jawzī transmit Muqātil; Baghawī, Qurtubī, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, Nasafī, Bursevī and Ālūsī describe the same binding and thrusting. Baghawī, Abū Ḥayyān and Biqāʿī add prodding from behind; Nasafī and Bursevī allow face-first or backward entry. Wāḥidī also reports the general exegetes' face-first account and Qatāda's violent hurrying. Study Quran adds dragging on faces, shackles, boiling liquid and cold murky fluid, citing 54:48, 40:71–72, 36:8, 40:70 and 38:57. ʿIṣlāḥī places the driving after the deniers' worldly pranks and before the rebuke for denial."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q06", "question": "What does Hell signify in the inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q06/p1", "position": "Hell is deprivation and pain deep in rebellious nature amid chains of attachment and bodily disposition.", "reasons": "Qāshānī gives this inward account while also glossing the verb as violent driving and dragging."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q07", "question": "What does the image of being pushed toward Hell convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q07/p1", "position": "It depicts terror and humiliation: keepers cast them from a distance, and frightened deniers are forced forward.", "reasons": "Rāzī says Hell is so terrifying that its keepers do not approach it but cast inmates from afar. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that terrified people fall back while assigned angels shove them onward. Biqāʿī says God appoints the agents of harsh driving and personifies Hell as a grimacing, loathing, coarse, roaring layer that receives them."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q08", "question": "What does the repeated verbal noun دَعًّا add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q08/p1", "position": "It confirms and intensifies the shove, presenting it as emphatically real and great in force.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the noun makes the push undeniable, comparing insistence that a weak run or trivial blow barely deserves its name. Biqāʿī says repetition of the root confirms and heightens the scene. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that the indefinite noun magnifies the act. ʿIṣlāḥī says the repeated verbal form increases the force and hatred."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q09", "question": "How is the next verse's statement ‘This is the Fire’ supplied here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q09/p1", "position": "An omitted saying introduces the guardians' words: ‘This is the Fire.’", "reasons": "Majāz expands the compressed wording as fa-yuqālu hādhihi al-nār. Samīn treats هذه النار as a nominal clause dependent on an implied saying verb and attributes the speech to the guardians. Rāzī makes the following declaration govern the day; Muqātil and ʿIṣlāḥī place the announcement after the shove."}]}

ough fire in 54:48?", "turns_on": "Whether 54:48 describes another fire, another angel's task, dragging by a chain from outside, or a later action inside the same Hell.", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q10/p1", "position": "The two descriptions appear to conflict: here they are pushed toward Hell, whereas 54:48 says they are dragged through fire.", "reasons": "Rāzī poses the difficulty before reporting four possible reconciliations."}, {"id": "52:13/q10/p2", "position": "They are dragged through one fire, then cast from a distance into another, hotter Hell.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 40:71–72 for dragging through boiling liquid before kindling in fire."}, {"id": "52:13/q10/p3", "position": "Different angels handle different stages: one pushes them toward fire and another drags them within it.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes the tasks or stages of the angels."}, {"id": "52:13/q10/p4", "position": "Chains allow them to be dragged inside while the angel pulling them remains outside.", "reasons": "Rāzī proposes this as a third reconciliation."}, {"id": "52:13/q10/p5", "position": "Angels push them in to humiliate them, then enter and drag them through Hell.", "reasons": "Rāzī offers this as a fourth possibility."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q11", "question": "What interpretive principles does ʿIṣlāḥī bring to this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q11/p1", "position": "He relies on the established muṣḥaf reading, Arab usage, discourse context and Qurʾānic parallels, aiming to protect readers from hostile misinterpretation.", "reasons": "ʿIṣlāḥī says his exegesis counters Orientalist, Jewish and extremist Shiite mischief; attentive readers will be protected. He says every Qurʾānic group is linked, each sūrah closely follows its predecessor, changing placement creates a gap, and removing a verse can damage its thematic sequence."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q13", "question": "When was Sūrah al-Ṭūr revealed?", "turns_on": "The notes offer both broad Makkan dating and a more specific sequence after al-Sajdah without arguing that they conflict.", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q13/p1", "position": "It is Makkan, probably from the latter half of the Makkan period.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports commentators' agreement on Makkan provenance and its likely later dating."}, {"id": "52:13/q13/p2", "position": "Some place its revelation immediately after Sūrah 32, al-Sajdah.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this chronology from some commentators, citing 32:1."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q14", "question": "Why is the sūrah called al-Ṭūr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q14/p1", "position": "Its title comes from the Mount in its first verse, usually understood as Mount Sinai.", "reasons": "Study Quran says most readers take al-Ṭūr as Sinai wherever it appears, citing 52:1, 2:63, 2:93, 19:52, 20:80, 28:29 and 28:46; it notes the fuller name in 23:20 and 95:2."}]}
{"id": "52:13/q15", "question": "How does this verse fit al-Ṭūr's opening and the preceding sūrahs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:13/q15/p1", "position": "It forms part of the opening warning of promised punishment and Judgment, developing the preceding sūrahs' proof of resurrection and the deniers' fate.", "reasons": "ʿIṣlāḥī places al-Ṭūr third after Qāf and al-Dhāriyāt, which prove resurrection and judgment by intellectual, historical, inward and outward evidence while presenting reward and punishment; he cites 51:5–6. He says 52:1–16 warns obstinate Quraysh through historical and universal facts, asserts punishment cannot be hastened or averted, and depicts Judgment. Study Quran links the opening half to 51:59–60 and the promises in 51:5 and 51:22; it describes the sequence from oaths and punishment to the reverent's reward, responses to charges against the Prophet, challenges to deniers, and closing counsel of patience and praise."}]}
{"id": "52:14/q01", "question": "What does the near demonstrative “this” indicate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:14/q01/p1", "position": "The Fire is immediately before the deniers, who have reached its edge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the near feminine demonstrative places them at Hell's edge and prepares for the following challenge about what they see."}]}
{"id": "52:14/q02", "question": "What is the Fire identified here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:14/q02/p1", "position": "It is the actual Hellfire and punishment they denied, now present before them.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī al-Wajīz calls it the very punishment denied. Biqāʿī describes the fire as a burning body that destroys what it touches and occupies its victims' attention, unlike their former play. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says its present reality fulfills what prophets foretold. The other cited sources identify it with the worldly deniers' rejected Fire."}]}
{"id": "52:14/q03", "question": "Who speaks the words “This is the Fire”?", "turns_on": "Whether the speakers are specifically Hell's keepers or the angels escorting the condemned; the Study Quran calls them angels without specifying their role.", "positions": [{"id": "52:14/q03/p1", "position": "Hell's keepers speak to the condemned.", "reasons": "Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and Bursawī identify the speakers as the keepers or guards of Hell; Ibn Kathīr calls their speech rebuke and reproach."}, {"id": "52:14/q03/p2", "position": "Angels address the punished; Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies them as the angels escorting the condemned.", "reasons": "The Study Quran attributes verses 14–16 to angels addressing the inhabitants of the Fire. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies the escorting angels as the speakers."}]}
{"id": "52:14/q04", "question": "How is the quoted speech introduced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:14/q04/p1", "position": "A verb of saying is omitted: they are told, “This is the Fire.”", "reasons": "Majāz reconstructs fa-yuqālu hādhihi al-nār. Zajjāj and Naḥḥās supply 'it is said to them'; Rāzī supplies an omitted qāla. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise read an unspoken introduction to quoted speech; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes the resulting reproach and Ibn ʿĀshūr draws the speaker from context."}]}

{"id": "52:14/q15", "question": "How is this passage held together within the sūrah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:14/q15/p1", "position": "Its verses form a coherent sequence under the sūrah's central theme.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says removing even one verse risks damaging the sequence. {"id": "52:14/q16", "question": "How does this sūrah connect with its predecessors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "52:14/q16/p1", "position": "Its received place after Qāf and al-Dhāriyāt continues their case for Judgment and punishment.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the Qur'an's present arrangement was set by God and His Prophet according to religious philosophy and divine-law wisdom rather than historical order, unlike the Torah and Gospel. {"id": "53:2/q01", "question": "Who is 'your companion,' and what does the description imply?", "turns_on": "Whether sahib stresses shared association or Muhammad's standing as master.", "positions": [{"id": "53:2/q01/p1", "position": "Muhammad, their familiar close associate.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Zajjaj, al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Alusi, al-Tabataba'i and Study Quran identify him. Al-Biqa'i, Bursevi, Elmalılı, Ibn Ashur, Kur'an Yolu and al-Samarra'i say Quraysh's long acquaintance with his honesty, sound mind, purity and care for them defeats its slander; Kur'an Yolu notes sohbet shares the root. {"id": "53:2/q02", "question": "What does 'did not stray' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether dalal is taken as departure from guidance or as madness.", "positions": [{"id": "53:2/q02/p1", "position": "He did not lose the path of truth and guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says he remained on a straight, sound course. Ibn Atiyya says the path God set him on. Razi says dalal may be broad enough to include any lost route. {"id": "53:2/q09", "question": "How does the cadence of the verse work?", "turns_on": "Which cadence pattern is valued and how sound is kept subordinate to meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "53:2/q09/p1", "position": "Its balanced clauses show the acceptable longer second cadence.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says equal clauses are finest because extra length after the expected endpoint feels heavy, yet 53:2 exemplifies a longer second clause; 69:30–31 illustrates a longer third. {"id": "53:2/q12", "question": "What does the denial establish about Muhammad's guidance and protection?", "turns_on": "How broadly the verse's guidance extends across life, conduct, and revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:2/q12/p1", "position": "He remained guided and morally protected throughout his life.", "reasons": "Razi says one destined for prophethood is preserved from unbelief and grave youthful vices; he applies the past tense to Muhammad's childhood and retreat.
